warmup.q: A table of fees has the rule CHECK (fee_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 1000): the database must refuse any row whose fee is outside 0 to 1000. The fee column may be left empty (NULL). A program saves a row with the fee left empty. What happens?
options: It's refused: an empty fee isn't between 0 and 1000
It's accepted: the check comes out unknown, and a CHECK refuses only false
It's accepted, and the fee is stored as 0
It's refused with an error saying the fee can't be empty
warmup.why: NULL BETWEEN 0 AND 1000 is unknown: in the three-valued logic of The relational model, keys and NULL, a comparison with an empty value is neither true nor false. A CHECK constraint refuses a row only when its condition is false, so unknown passes. WHERE is the mirror image: it keeps a row only when its condition is true. To refuse an empty fee, the column also needs NOT NULL. The first option is the tempting one, because "between 0 and 1000" sounds as if it shuts out everything else.

sections.html:
A partner bank, another company that handles card payments for some of the same shops, sends a file of payments every night. The quickest way to load it is to keep it exactly as it arrives: one row per payment, with every detail on every row. That's the table payments_export. Here are 5 of its 10 columns:

course=# SELECT payment_id, customer_name, merchant_name, mcc, mcc_description
course-# FROM payments_export
course-# ORDER BY payment_id;
 payment_id | customer_name |   merchant_name   | mcc  |       mcc_description
------------+---------------+-------------------+------+------------------------------
         13 | Ben Carter    | Harbor Hotel      | 7011 | Hotels, motels, resorts
         14 | Asha Rao      | Northwind Grocers | 5411 | Grocery stores, supermarkets
         15 | Elena Petrova | Volt Electronics  | 5732 | Electronics stores
         16 | Jonas Weber   | Harbor Hotel      | 7011 | Hotels, motels, resorts
         17 | Farid Hadad   | Volt Electronics  | 5732 | Electronics stores
         18 | Farid Haddad  | Volt Electronics  | 5732 | Electronic stores
         19 | Chloe Martin  | Volt Electronics  | 5732 | Electronics stores
         20 | Ben Carter    | Northwind Grocers | 5411 | Grocery stores, supermarkets
         21 | Mateo Ruiz    | Quick Bite        | 5812 | Eating places, restaurants
         22 | Jonas Weber   | Harbor Hotel      | 7011 | Hotels, motels, resorts
(10 rows)

The mcc is the merchant category code: a four-digit number the card companies give each shop to say what kind of business it is. Volt Electronics is in category 5732, electronics shops, and the file says so four times in ten rows. A year of files would say it once for every Volt payment, perhaps 50,000 times. Each copy is a chance to disagree, and this small file already disagrees twice. Payment 17 spells Farid's surname with one d. Payment 18 calls category 5732 "Electronic stores". Which spelling is right? The table can't tell you, because it stores the same fact in several places and nothing keeps the copies equal.

That's the café's order book again. Storing a fact many times does three kinds of damage, and each has a name. A fact stored on many rows must be changed on all of them, and missing one leaves the table contradicting itself, as it does here. That's an update anomaly, where an anomaly is something wrong that the design allows. You also can't record a fact on its own. Category 5814 means "Fast food restaurants", but there's nowhere to write that down until a payment at a fast-food shop arrives: an insert anomaly. And deleting one fact can delete another. Payment 21 is the only Quick Bite row in the file. Delete it, say because it turned out to be fraud, and you also lose the fact that Quick Bite is a restaurant: a delete anomaly.

The fix is to store each fact once and point at it from everywhere else. That's what keys are for. A key is a column, or a set of columns, whose value names exactly one row, so another table can refer to that row by its key. The order book could have written "customer 17" on each line, and kept one card per customer with the name and the phone number. Deciding which facts get a table of their own is called normalization. The Try it below finds the two disagreements with a query, and the next section turns the hunt into a method.

try.title: Find the disagreements
steps: Start the database if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d from the labs folder) and open psql: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.

Run the first query. It puts the rows into one group per email (GROUP BY), counts the different names in each group, and keeps only the groups with more than one name (HAVING). Predict how many emails come back.
Run the second. Does every shop name come with exactly one category code?

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SELECT customer_email, count(DISTINCT customer_name) AS names, min(customer_name), max(customer_name) FROM payments_export GROUP BY customer_email HAVING count(DISTINCT customer_name) > 1; SELECT merchant_name, count(DISTINCT mcc) AS codes FROM payments_export GROUP BY merchant_name HAVING count(DISTINCT mcc) > 1;

try.expect:
The first query finds one email with two names:

      customer_email      | names |     min     |     max
--------------------------+-------+-------------+--------------
 farid.haddad@example.com |     2 | Farid Hadad | Farid Haddad
(1 row)

The second returns (0 rows): in this file, every shop name maps to one code. min and max show the two spellings, the first and the last in alphabetical order. Aggregation, lesson 4 of this track, covers GROUP BY and HAVING in depth.

sections.h: Functional dependencies show where to cut
sections.html:
How do you decide which facts get a table of their own? Start with a promise about the data, in plain words: every row with the email farid.haddad@example.com should have the same customer name. One email, one name. That promise is a functional dependency, written customer_email → customer_name and read "email determines name". In general, X → Y means that any two rows that agree on X also agree on Y.

You find dependencies by asking what the columns mean, not by staring at the data. Then you test them against the data, with the query from the Try it: group the rows by X and look for a group with more than one Y. One such group, and the promise is broken.

A key is the strongest dependency there is. payment_id determines every other column of the export, because it names one payment. The trouble starts with dependencies whose left side isn't a key. The export has three:

  • customer_email → customer_name
  • merchant_name → mcc
  • mcc → mcc_description

Each is a fact about something other than the payment: a person, a shop, a category. Yet each is stored again on every payment row. The figure shows the pattern. payment_id → merchant_name → mcc → mcc_description is a chain, and its far end repeats for every payment of every shop in that category.

The cure is mechanical, which is good news. Take each dependency whose left side isn't a key. Move its columns into a new table, and make the left side that table's primary key. The payments table keeps only the column that points at the new table. Do that three times and you get customers (email → name), merchants (shop → category) and mcc_codes (category → description). What's left is payments, with the payment's own facts and a key for each of the others. That's the course's own schema, its set of tables and their rules. It uses numbers such as merchant_id as keys instead of names, but the split is the same.

The normal forms are names for how far along this road a table is. Each one adds a rule to the one before:

  1. First normal form (1NF): every column holds one value. No "visa,amex" in one column, and no card1, card2, card3 columns.
  2. Second normal form (2NF): no column depends on only part of a key made of several columns. Take a table of nightly payouts to shops, daily_payouts(payout_day, merchant_id, merchant_name, amount), keyed by (payout_day, merchant_id). merchant_name depends on merchant_id alone, so the table breaks 2NF. A table whose key is one column, like the export with payment_id, is in 2NF automatically.
  3. Third normal form (3NF): no column depends on another column outside the key. The export fails here, through the chain in the figure.
  4. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF): the left side of every dependency is a candidate key, a smallest set of columns that never repeats. It differs from 3NF only in rare tables with overlapping candidate keys.

Aim for BCNF by default. It costs a join, a query step that puts rows from two tables side by side, each time you read the facts back together. That's the next lesson. In return, you never have to decide which of two spellings is true.

One fact, one place. Cut wherever a column outside the key decides another.

Storing every fact once has a price, though: some questions must now add up many rows to get one number. Next, we'll keep one copy on purpose and see what it costs.

mcc determines mcc_description; customer_email determines customer_name."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box-a" x="20" y="100" width="120" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="80.0" y="123" text-anchor="middle">payment_id</text><rect class="box" x="200" y="30" width="150" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="275.0" y="53" text-anchor="middle">merchant_name</text><rect class="box" x="400" y="30" width="90" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="445.0" y="53" text-anchor="middle">mcc</text><rect class="box" x="530" y="30" width="150" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="605.0" y="53" text-anchor="middle">mcc_description</text><rect class="box" x="200" y="100" width="150" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="275.0" y="123" text-anchor="middle">customer_email</text><rect class="box" x="400" y="100" width="150" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="475.0" y="123" text-anchor="middle">customer_name</text><rect class="box" x="200" y="170" width="230" height="36" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="315.0" y="193" text-anchor="middle">amount_minor, created_at</text><line class="ln" x1="140" y1="112" x2="198" y2="54" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln" x1="140" y1="118" x2="198" y2="118" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln" x1="140" y1="124" x2="198" y2="182" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="350" y1="48" x2="398" y2="48" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="490" y1="48" x2="528" y2="48" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="350" y1="118" x2="398" y2="118" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="240" text-anchor="start">white: the key decides it.  blue: a non-key column decides it, so the fact repeats on every row.</text></svg>
figure.caption: The dependencies in payments_export. Each blue arrow starts at a column that isn't a key, so its fact repeats on every row, and each one becomes a table of its own.

try.title: Test a dependency, then break the load
steps: Run the first query. It lists each different pair of category and description once. If mcc → mcc_description held, each mcc would appear once.
Now try to build a table of categories from the file. CREATE TABLE makes a new table, and INSERT INTO ... SELECT fills it with a query's answer. Predict which statement fails, and why.
ROLLBACK drops the new table again: in PostgreSQL, even CREATE TABLE is part of the transaction.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SELECT DISTINCT mcc, mcc_description FROM payments_export ORDER BY mcc; BEGIN; CREATE TABLE export_mcc (mcc text PRIMARY KEY, description text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO export_mcc SELECT DISTINCT mcc, mcc_description FROM payments_export; ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
5732 appears twice, with "Electronics stores" and "Electronic stores". The CREATE TABLE succeeds, and the INSERT fails on the primary key:

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "export_mcc_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (mcc)=(5732) already exists.

The key on mcc is the dependency mcc → description turned into a rule. Once the table exists, the second spelling has nowhere to go.

sections.h: Keep a copy on purpose, and check it
sections.html:
Normalization says: store a fact once, and work everything else out from it. Take an account's balance. The app keeps a ledger, the table ledger_entries: a book of every movement of money, one row per movement, never rubbed out. A deposit into an account is a row, and a payment out of it is another. The balance is the sum of the account's rows. Every tap of a card asks "does this account have enough money?", so the app would add up that sum on every tap. How expensive is that?

On the course's large data set, which later lessons load (3.4 million ledger rows), adding up account 42's 46 rows without an index takes about 42 ms, thousandths of a second. PostgreSQL reads every row in the table to find those 46. With an index on account_id, a sorted lookup structure like the one behind a key, it drops to about 0.3 ms. That's fine for account 42. But the company's own clearing account, which every deposit passes through, has 750,000 rows, so even with the index, its sum reads 750,000 rows. Reading one stored number takes about 0.015 ms. (Times from an Apple-silicon laptop running Docker Desktop. Yours will differ with the CPU and disk, but the ratios hold.)

So normalized and denormalized are two ends of one trade. A normalized schema makes writes cheap and safe, because each fact lives in one place, and it makes some reads pay: a join, or a sum over many rows. A copy turns that read into one lookup, and moves the cost to every write, which must now update the copy too.

Normalize by default. Keep a copy only for a read you've measured.

So the course schema keeps one copy on purpose: accounts.balance_minor holds the sum of the account's ledger rows. Storing a value you could work out is called denormalization, and it brings back the update anomaly from the first section. Every new ledger row now needs two writes, the row and the balance, and they must agree. Here are three ways to keep them in step, from best to worst:

  1. Write both in the same transaction, a group of changes saved all together or not at all. Either both happen or neither does.
  2. Let a trigger update the balance: a small function the database itself runs whenever a row is added.
  3. Update the balance from the app after the ledger row is saved. A crash between the two steps leaves them apart for good.

Whichever you choose, add a check that adds up the ledger again and compares the total with the copy. A café does the same every night when it counts the till against the day's receipts, and bookkeepers call it reconciliation. The check runs on a schedule, and it's the lab's third exercise. The Try it shows a copy drifting. Look closely at account 112 in its output, because that row is where such checks go wrong.

The balance is derived data, a copy worked out from the record. It's only as honest as the code that writes it and the check that guards it. The database can keep some copies by itself: the generated column in Go deeper, and the materialized views (stored answers to queries) of the Storage engines track. A copy kept in another program for fast reads, a cache, shares no transaction with the ledger at all. Redis, a program that keeps data in memory, is a common home for one, and Keeping a cache honest, in the Caching and in-memory data track, starts there.

Two details in the Try it's output matter later. sum of a bigint column, a column of large whole numbers, returns numeric, a decimal number with as many digits as it needs, so the total can't overflow. And, from the last lesson, sum over no rows returns NULL, not 0.

A copy drifts when a writer skips a step, and nothing stops the writer. Next, we'll let the database stop bad writes itself.

try.title: Make the balance drift
steps: Type \pset null '∅'. Then look at journal 3. A journal is one movement of money, written as ledger rows that add up to zero: here, a deposit of 300.00 leaves the clearing account 900 and arrives in account 103.
Start a transaction and post a new deposit of 10.00 to account 103, without touching accounts.
Compare each balance with its ledger sum for accounts 103, 112 and 900. Predict: what will a check like balance_minor <> ledger say about account 112?
ROLLBACK when you're done.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: \pset null '∅' SELECT account_id, entry_type, amount_minor, created_at FROM ledger_entries WHERE journal_id = 3; BEGIN; INSERT INTO ledger_entries (journal_id, account_id, entry_type, amount_minor, created_at) VALUES (3001, 103, 'deposit', 1000, now()), (3001, 900, 'deposit', -1000, now()); SELECT a.account_id, a.balance_minor, (SELECT sum(e.amount_minor) FROM ledger_entries e WHERE e.account_id = a.account_id) AS ledger FROM accounts a WHERE a.account_id IN (103, 112, 900) ORDER BY a.account_id; ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
account_id | balance_minor | ledger
------------+---------------+---------
        103 |          9086 |   10086
        112 |             0 |       ∅
        900 |       -860000 | -861000
(3 rows)

Accounts 103 and 900 have drifted by 1000 cents, in opposite directions. Account 112 has no ledger rows, so its sum is NULL, and 0 <> NULL is unknown. A check that compares the two directly will never report account 112, whatever its balance says.

sections.h: Constraints are rules the server checks on every write
sections.html:
The app checks each payment before it saves it: is the amount positive, does the card exist? That's not enough. Other programs write to the same tables: a script that fixes old data, a person typing into psql, a second copy of the app, a request that arrives twice. None of them runs the app's checks. And two requests can pass the same check at the same moment, and both save. The only place where a rule holds for every writer is the database, at the moment of the write. A constraint is such a rule. Let's build them up from the simplest.

NOT NULL refuses an empty value. Use it on every column that must always have one, which is most of them.

CHECK (condition) refuses a row for which the condition is false. Remember the three-valued logic of the last lesson: a CHECK fails only on false. So an empty fee passes CHECK (fee_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 1000), because the condition is unknown. Put NOT NULL next to every CHECK whose column must have a value. A CHECK also sees one row at a time. "A payment's refunds never add up to more than the payment" depends on other rows, so it can't be a CHECK. That rule needs a trigger, or the app plus row locks, which make other writers wait their turn. Lost updates, in the Transactions track, covers them.

UNIQUE refuses a second row with the same values. By default, two NULLs count as different, so a UNIQUE column accepts any number of NULLs. PostgreSQL 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT to allow only one.

PRIMARY KEY is UNIQUE plus NOT NULL, once per table.

REFERENCES is the foreign key from the last lesson: the value must exist as a key in another table. It also decides what happens when someone deletes the row it points at. The default, NO ACTION, refuses the delete while anything still points at the row. CASCADE deletes the pointing rows too, and SET NULL empties their reference. For money, keep the default: deleting a shop must never quietly delete its payments.

Types are constraints too. Store money as bigint cents, never as float, the computer's binary fractions, in which 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3. Avoid PostgreSQL's money type too, because how it reads and prints amounts depends on a setting for the local currency. Store instants as timestamptz, and text as text, with a CHECK when it needs a format. CHECK (country_code ~ '^[A-Z]{2}$') uses a pattern, a regular expression, that means "exactly two capital letters".

One more behaviour surprises people. Identity columns take their numbers from a sequence, and a sequence never gives a number back: an insert that fails still uses one up. So ids have gaps, and they're never a count.

A rule in the app holds for the app. A rule in the table holds for everyone.

Each of these rules looks at one row, or compares a new value with stored ones for equality. Next, we'll meet a rule that needs more: two fees in force on the same day.

try.title: Watch the server say no
steps: Run the block one statement at a time. Before each INSERT, predict: accepted or refused? (fee_bps is a fee in basis points, hundredths of a percent.)
After ROLLBACK, run \d fee_overrides. Is the table still there?
Run the DELETE, which removes rows. Shop 6 has no payments. Why does it still fail?

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: \pset null '∅' BEGIN; CREATE TABLE fee_overrides ( merchant_id bigint REFERENCES merchants, fee_bps int CHECK (fee_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 1000) ); INSERT INTO fee_overrides VALUES (1, NULL), (NULL, 250); SELECT * FROM fee_overrides; INSERT INTO fee_overrides VALUES (1, 2000); ROLLBACK; \d fee_overrides DELETE FROM merchants WHERE merchant_id = 6;

try.expect:
Both NULL rows are accepted. The CHECK is unknown for the first, and an empty foreign key points at nothing, so there's nothing to check for the second. The fee of 2000 is refused:

ERROR:  new row for relation "fee_overrides" violates check constraint "fee_overrides_fee_bps_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (1, 2000).

After ROLLBACK, \d prints Did not find any relation named "fee_overrides". The table vanished with the transaction. The DELETE fails because shop 6 has an account, 306, where its takings land, and that account points at it:

ERROR:  update or delete on table "merchants" violates foreign key constraint "accounts_merchant_id_fkey" on table "accounts"
DETAIL:  Key (merchant_id)=(6) is still referenced from table "accounts".

refs.title: PostgreSQL wiki: Don't Do This (money, serial, varchar(n))

sections.h: Time ranges that must not overlap
sections.html:
The company charges each shop a small fee on every payment, and the fee changes over time. Fees are written in basis points, hundredths of a percent. Shop 1, Northwind Grocers, paid 290 basis points (2.90%) until 1 July 2026, and 250 after it. To work out the fee on a payment, you need exactly one fee in force at its moment. So store the periods, and then make overlaps impossible.

Simplest version: two columns, valid_from and valid_to, with CHECK (valid_from < valid_to) and UNIQUE (merchant_id, valid_from). It refuses two periods that start on the same day. It accepts January to July plus June to September, which both cover 15 June. A UNIQUE constraint compares a new row with stored rows for equality only, and two overlapping periods aren't equal.

Next try: check in the app before saving. "Look up this shop's periods, and save the new one only if none overlaps." Two people at the company save at the same moment. Both look, both see no overlap, and both save, like two colleagues who each check that the meeting room is free and then both book it. That's a check-then-act race: the check and the save are two steps, and another writer can act between them.

The database has to compare the new period with the stored ones itself, at the moment of the insert. PostgreSQL stores a period as a range type. tstzrange holds a start instant and an end instant, written [2026-01-01,2026-07-01). The square bracket includes the start, the round bracket leaves out the end (a half-open range, as in the last lesson), and an empty end means "no end yet". The operator && asks whether two ranges overlap, and @> asks whether a range contains an instant. With those, the rule fits in one line. PostgreSQL 18 added temporal keys, keys that understand periods of time:

PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, valid_during WITHOUT OVERLAPS)

It means: for each merchant_id, no two valid_during ranges may overlap. PostgreSQL keeps the key in a GiST index, a search tree built for questions like "which stored ranges overlap this one?", and checks it on every insert and update. Before version 18, you wrote the same rule as an exclusion constraint: EXCLUDE USING gist (merchant_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&). It reads "no two rows where merchant_id is equal and the ranges overlap". Both need btree_gist, an add-on (an extension) that lets a plain number sit in a GiST index, and the course schema installs it. Both fail with error code 23P01, from SQLSTATE, the standard list of SQL error codes. One difference: WITHOUT OVERLAPS also refuses an empty range, and EXCLUDE accepts it.

Finding the fee for a payment is then one lookup: WHERE merchant_id = 4 AND valid_during @> timestamptz '2026-03-12 16:40+00' returns 280.

An overlap is a question about other rows. Let the database answer it.

We now have tables that each hold one kind of fact, and rules that keep bad rows out. But a payment row now says card 8 and shop 4, and the names live in other tables.

stepper.title: A temporal key checks every insert
stepper.intro: Merchants 6 and 8, two shops, have no fee periods yet. Click Next to insert rows and watch which ones the key accepts.

try.title: Insert three fee periods
steps: Look at merchant 1's two periods. They touch at 1 July 2026. Predict which of the three inserts for merchant 6 fails.
Run the block. After the error, PostgreSQL refuses to run anything more in this transaction, so ROLLBACK it.
Run \d merchant_fee_schedules and find the key.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SELECT * FROM merchant_fee_schedules WHERE merchant_id = 1 ORDER BY valid_during; BEGIN; INSERT INTO merchant_fee_schedules VALUES (6, '[2026-01-01,2026-07-01)', 300); INSERT INTO merchant_fee_schedules VALUES (6, '[2026-07-01,)', 280); INSERT INTO merchant_fee_schedules VALUES (6, '[2026-06-01,2026-09-01)', 310); ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
The first two inserts print INSERT 0 1, which means one row was added. The third fails:

ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "merchant_fee_schedules_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (merchant_id, valid_during)=(6, ["2026-06-01 00:00:00+00","2026-09-01 00:00:00+00")) conflicts with existing key (merchant_id, valid_during)=(6, ["2026-01-01 00:00:00+00","2026-07-01 00:00:00+00")).

The message calls the primary key an exclusion constraint, because that's how PostgreSQL builds it. \d lists it as "merchant_fee_schedules_pkey" PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, valid_during WITHOUT OVERLAPS).

opening:
Picture a café's old order book. For every order, the barista wrote the customer's name, phone number, drink and price on one line. Then a regular changes her phone number. Her number now sits on 200 lines, and someone has to change all of them. They change 199.

Now the book says two different things, and nobody can tell which is right. The trap is easy to fall into, because writing everything on every line is the fastest way to record it, and on the first day it works perfectly. The trouble starts only when a fact changes.

In The relational model, keys and NULL, keys told us which row is which. They didn't tell us which facts deserve a table of their own. In this lesson, we'll take a messy file of payments, find the facts it repeats, split it so each fact lives in one place, keep one copy on purpose, and teach the database to refuse bad rows. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café order book where a phone number lived on 200 lines, and one line was missed. A table has the same weakness. The cure is to store each fact once, keyed by what decides it, and let the database refuse bad rows. The one copy we kept on purpose, the balance, comes with a nightly check.

In psql, run \d accounts and read its rules: which columns are NOT NULL, which CHECKs run, which keys point elsewhere. Then think of a form you filled in this week: which of its rules would a database enforce?

Next, we'll put the tables back together, and ask how one query turns card 8 and shop 4 into "Farid Haddad paid Volt Electronics 189.99".

compare.title: The same table, and a failed change, in Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle
a.html: CREATE TABLE refunds ( refund_id NUMBER(19) GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, payment_id NUMBER(19) NOT NULL REFERENCES payments, amount_minor NUMBER(19) NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0), reason VARCHAR2(20 CHAR) NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL ); -- DDL commits implicitly, before and after each statement. -- A migration that fails on its third statement -- leaves the first two applied.

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.html: CREATE TABLE refunds ( refund_id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, payment_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES payments, amount_minor bigint NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0), reason text NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL ); -- DDL is transactional: inside BEGIN ... COMMIT, -- an error on the third statement rolls back -- all three.

compare.note: Oracle Database is a commercial database program that many large companies run. The column types map one to one. NUMBER(19) becomes bigint, and VARCHAR2(n CHAR) becomes text (add a CHECK on length() if the limit is a real rule). Both accept the standard GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (Oracle since version 12c). What differs is how changes to tables behave inside a transaction. Statements that create or change tables, such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP, are called DDL. Oracle commits before and after every DDL statement, so a change script that fails halfway stays half done, and you repair it by hand. PostgreSQL runs DDL inside the transaction like any INSERT. Tools that apply numbered change scripts, called migrations, wrap each PostgreSQL migration in a transaction (Flyway is one such tool), so a failed one leaves no trace. A few statements, such as CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, can't run inside a transaction.

worked.title: From the partner's flat file to a table that guards one fact

steps.say: Write down the dependencies you expect from what the columns mean, then test each one. A dependency X → Y fails when some X has more than one Y. The email test finds Farid's two spellings.
steps.code: -- 1. test customer_email -> customer_name SELECT customer_email, count(DISTINCT customer_name) AS names FROM payments_export GROUP BY customer_email HAVING count(DISTINCT customer_name) > 1; -- farid.haddad@example.com | 2

steps.say: Name the key and follow the chain. payment_id determines everything, and merchant_name → mcc → mcc_description hangs off it. The far end of the chain becomes the first new table, with the left side of the dependency as its primary key. The CHECK says an mcc is exactly four digits.
steps.code: -- 2. one fact, one table: the left side is the key CREATE TABLE export_mcc ( mcc text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (mcc ~ '^[0-9]{4}$'), description text NOT NULL );

steps.say:
Load it. The primary key refuses the second spelling of 5732, so the load fails instead of picking one at random:

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "export_mcc_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (mcc)=(5732) already exists.

This is the key doing its job. SELECT DISTINCT ON or min(mcc_description) would make the error go away, and quietly keep whichever spelling sorts first.
steps.code: -- 3. load: fails on 5732 INSERT INTO export_mcc SELECT DISTINCT mcc, mcc_description FROM payments_export;

steps.say: Decide which spelling is true (the card companies' list says "Electronics stores"), fix the rows in the file's table and load again. Four codes go in: INSERT 0 4. From now on, a fifth spelling has nowhere to live.
steps.code: -- 4. fix the data, then load UPDATE payments_export SET mcc_description = 'Electronics stores' WHERE mcc = '5732' AND mcc_description <> 'Electronics stores'; -- UPDATE 1 INSERT INTO export_mcc SELECT DISTINCT mcc, mcc_description FROM payments_export;

lab.title: Test a dependency, build a table that refuses bad rows, catch a drifting copy
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Most of the eleven fail for now. Each test runs in a transaction that's rolled back at the end, so the tables you create vanish after every test.
In mcc_description_conflicts.sql, list each mcc in payments_export that has more than one description, with the count.
In card_limits.sql, replace the CREATE TABLE so the database refuses every bad row the comment lists: unknown cards, NULLs, limits outside 1 to 10,000,000 cents, and overlapping periods for one card.
In balance_drift.sql, fix the check so it also reports an account that has a balance but no ledger rows.
Run the tests until all eleven pass. Try your table in psql first, inside BEGIN and ROLLBACK.
hints: The card limit tests accept error code 23P01 (exclusion) or 23505 (unique) for an overlap, so either WITHOUT OVERLAPS or EXCLUDE USING gist passes.
A CHECK passes on NULL. The NULL tests need NOT NULL on all three columns.
coalesce(x, 0) returns x, or 0 when x is NULL. Work out the ledger sum in a subquery, then compare.

drill.title: Write the fee schedule table from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the CREATE TABLE for merchant_fee_schedules: a shop (merchant_id), a period and a fee in basis points from 0 to 1000. No shop may have two periods in force at once. Write the PostgreSQL 18 key, then the exclusion constraint you'd use on PostgreSQL 17.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE merchant_fee_schedules ( merchant_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES merchants, valid_during tstzrange NOT NULL, -- [from, to), open end allowed fee_bps int NOT NULL CHECK (fee_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 1000), PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, valid_during WITHOUT OVERLAPS) -- PostgreSQL 18 ); -- PostgreSQL 17 and older (CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist first): -- EXCLUDE USING gist (merchant_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&)

recap: A fact stored on many rows drifts: update, insert and delete anomalies all come from repetition.
A functional dependency X → Y says rows that agree on X agree on Y. Find them from what the columns mean, and test them with GROUP BY X HAVING count(DISTINCT Y) > 1.
Normalize by moving every dependency whose left side isn't a key into its own table, keyed by that left side. BCNF is the target, and the price is a join when you read.
Keep a copy (denormalize) only for a read you've measured. Write it in the same transaction as the record, and run a check that compares the two and handles NULL sums.

Constraints are the only rules every writer obeys. A CHECK passes on NULL, so pair it with NOT NULL. PRIMARY KEY (id, period WITHOUT OVERLAPS) (PostgreSQL 18) or EXCLUDE USING gist stops overlapping ranges, which UNIQUE can't.

The limit: a constraint sees one row, or compares a new row with stored ones by fixed tests. A rule across many rows, such as refunds never exceeding their payment, still needs a trigger or locks, and the split tables must be joined again to answer most questions.

explain.prompt: A friend who's new to databases asks why the course has a separate mcc_codes table, when the partner bank's file already carries the description on every row. Explain it to them with the file's own data, and say what the primary key on mcc_codes adds.
explain.answer: In the file, the description depends on the category code, not on the payment, so it's repeated on every payment of every shop in that category. Repeated facts drift: the file already calls 5732 both "Electronics stores" and "Electronic stores", and nothing says which is right. You also can't record a category before a payment uses it, and deleting the last payment of a category loses its description. Moving mcc → description into its own table stores the fact once. The primary key on mcc turns the dependency into a rule: a second description for 5732 is refused when someone tries to insert it, instead of being stored.

deeper.html:
Three PostgreSQL 18 features in the course schema are worth a closer look.

The first is the virtual generated column. payments.amount_major is declared numeric(21, 2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (amount_minor / 100.0). In PostgreSQL 18, a generated column is VIRTUAL by default: it takes no space on disk and is worked out when you read it. Add STORED to work it out on write and keep it on disk, which was the only kind before 18. A generated column is denormalization that the database keeps in step for you, because nobody can write to it.

The second is UUIDv7 keys. payment_uid defaults to uuidv7(), new in PostgreSQL 18. A version 7 UUID starts with the time it was made, in milliseconds, so new ids sort after old ones and land at the right-hand end of the B-tree index. Random version 4 UUIDs land anywhere in the index, so each insert can touch a different page. The seed, the set of made-up rows the course database starts with, builds its uids from created_at, so you can read the time back:

course=# SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, amount_major, uuid_extract_timestamp(payment_uid) AS uid_time, created_at
course-# FROM payments WHERE payment_id IN (1, 22);
 payment_id | amount_minor | amount_major |         uid_time         |        created_at
------------+--------------+--------------+--------------------------+--------------------------
          1 |         4250 |        42.50 | 2026-01-03 10:12:00+00   | 2026-01-03 10:12:00+00
         22 |        52000 |       520.00 | 2026-03-31 23:59:59.5+00 | 2026-03-31 23:59:59.5+00
(2 rows)

The time inside a UUIDv7 is visible to anyone who sees the id. If creation times are sensitive, don't show v7 ids outside your own system.

The third is temporal foreign keys. A table can now point at a temporal key with PERIOD: FOREIGN KEY (merchant_id, PERIOD valid_during) REFERENCES merchant_fee_schedules (merchant_id, PERIOD valid_during) requires the periods it points at to cover the pointing row's whole period. It doesn't support ON DELETE CASCADE or SET NULL. The CREATE TABLE page in the PostgreSQL 18 documentation has the details.

Normal forms go further than BCNF. 4NF and 5NF deal with independent facts that each have several values, kept in one table, such as a shop's card brands and its currencies stored as every combination. You'll rarely need them if every table stores facts about one thing.
